etymology: A compound of hate and speech. The Oxford English Dictionary records its earliest evidence in 1938, in the Syracuse (New York) Herald. The words are old and plain; the bending is in how the phrase is defined and used.
biblical_def: Hate speech is commonly defined as speech that expresses hatred of, or encourages violence against, a person or group because of race, religion, sex, sexual orientation or a similar trait. It has no single, consistent definition, and legal definitions vary from country to country. In the United States most of what is called hate speech is constitutionally protected. In Matal v. Tam (2017) the Supreme Court said that speech demeaning people on the basis of race, religion and similar grounds “is hateful; but the proudest boast of our free speech jurisprudence is that we protect the freedom to express ‘the thought that we hate.’” The Christian observation: Scripture takes hateful words more seriously than any statute does. Christ said that whoever calls his brother a fool “shall be in danger of hell fire” (Mat 5:22), and John wrote that “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer” (1Jn 3:15). But Scripture also commands a holy hatred: “The fear of the LORD is to hate evil” (Pro 8:13); “Hate the evil, and love the good” (Amo 5:15). And Christ told His brothers that the world hated Him “because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil” (Joh 7:7).
webster_summary: Speech that expresses hatred of, or incites violence against, a person or group for a shared trait (OED earliest 1938); no single definition exists. Scripture forbids hating a brother (1Jn 3:15) and commands hating evil (Amo 5:15).
webster_full: HATE SPEECH, n. (from 1938, OED) Speech expressing hatred of, or encouraging violence against, a person or group on account of race, religion, sex, sexual orientation or a similar characteristic. Compound of hate + speech.
Usage note: the term has no single, consistent definition; in the United States most speech so labelled is constitutionally protected (Wikipedia, “Hate speech”; Matal v. Tam, 2017).
scriptures: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph.
The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil.
corruption_summary: Hate speech has no fixed definition, so whoever holds the definition decides what may be said; it is now routinely applied to plain statements of biblical morality, recasting testimony against sin as hatred of persons.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the phrase has no single definition, its edges move with whoever is applying it. A category that began with incitement to violence has been stretched to cover disagreement, and the man who says that Scripture calls a practice sin is told that he has spoken hate. The label does the work an argument should do, and it makes the speaker, not the claim, the thing on trial.

Scripture draws the line in a different place. Hatred of a brother is murder in the heart (1Jn 3:15), and the Christian must repent of it wherever it is found in him. But testimony that the works of the world are evil is not hatred; it is what Christ did, and the world hated Him for it (Joh 7:7). To call evil good and good evil is the woe of Isa 5:20. The church must keep both commands: love the sinner as a neighbour, and hate the evil (Amo 5:15).
roots_summary: hate + speech → hate speech (OED earliest 1938) → group-libel campaigns after World War II → elastic modern label with no fixed definition.
roots_lines: 1940s–1950s: American civil rights groups press for restrictions on hateful speech, framed as group libel (Wikipedia)
2017: Matal v. Tam: the Supreme Court protects “the thought that we hate”
usage: “The post was removed as hate speech, though it only quoted the passage.”
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil. (Pro 8:13).
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. (1Jn 3:15).

etymology: Formed within English by conversion from the combining form -phobia, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1786, in the Columbian Magazine. The combining form comes from Greek phobos, “fear.”
biblical_def: A phobia is a fear: in its proper, clinical sense, an excessive or irrational dread of something. The word came into English from the suffix -phobia, from Greek phobos, fear. In the twentieth century the suffix was attached to political and moral disagreement. The best-known example, homophobia, was coined by the psychologist George Weinberg in the 1960s and first appeared in print in 1969. In 1980 the researchers Hudson and Ricketts proposed a different term because they regarded homophobia as unscientific in its presumption of motivation. The Christian observation: Scripture names two fears. One is commanded: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7). The other is cast out: “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind” (2Ti 1:7). Christ joins them: “fear not them which kill the body… but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28).
webster_summary: An excessive or irrational fear (OED earliest 1786, from -phobia, Greek phobos); now attached as a suffix to moral disagreement, recasting conviction as pathology. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Pro 1:7).
webster_full: PHOBIA, n. (from 1786, OED) An excessive or irrational fear or aversion. From the combining form -phobia, Greek phobos, fear.
Usage note: homophobia was coined by George Weinberg in the 1960s; Hudson and Ricketts (1980) called it unscientific in its presumption of motivation (Wikipedia, “Homophobia”).
scriptures: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
corruption_summary: The -phobia suffix turns moral judgment into a diagnosis: the man who believes God’s law is said to be afraid or sick, so his reasons need never be answered.
corruption_paragraphs: A phobia is a disorder, and disorders are treated, not debated. That is why the suffix is so effective in a moral argument. Once a Christian’s conviction about marriage or sexuality is called a phobia, the conversation moves from whether he is right to what is wrong with him. Researchers Hudson and Ricketts, in a 1980 paper, called the term unscientific in its presumption of motivation.

Scripture does not call conviction fear. It calls the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge (Pro 1:7) and says that God has given His people a sound mind, not a spirit of fear (2Ti 1:7). To relabel faithfulness as sickness is to call good evil (Isa 5:20). The Christian answers the label by speaking with love and a sound mind, and by refusing to accept the diagnosis.
roots_summary: Greek phobos, fear → -phobia → phobia (OED earliest 1786) → clinical term → political suffix (homophobia, coined 1960s).
roots_lines: 1960s: George Weinberg coins homophobia; first in print 1969 (Wikipedia)
1980: Hudson and Ricketts call the term unscientific in its presumption of motivation (Wikipedia)
usage: “Disagreeing with him is not a phobia; give me an argument.”
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind. (2Ti 1:7).

etymology: Formed within English from the prefix mis- and information. The Oxford English Dictionary records its earliest evidence in 1587, in a text by Abraham Fleming, author, literary editor and Church of England clergyman, and others. It is an old and plain word; the bending is modern.
biblical_def: Misinformation is incorrect or misleading information. The word is more than four centuries old and was long a plain one: a man was misinformed, and when he learned better he was corrected. Modern usage separates it from disinformation: misinformation may be spread with or without intent to deceive, while disinformation is deliberately deceptive. In January 2024 the World Economic Forum named misinformation and disinformation the most severe global risks in the short term. The Christian observation: God cares about truth, and so must His people. “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16). The remedy Scripture gives for error is examination, not a label: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The Bereans were called noble because they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), even when the man teaching them was an apostle.
webster_summary: Incorrect or misleading information (OED earliest 1587), spread with or without intent to deceive. Once a plain word for error, it is now often an official label that ends a question instead of examining it. Scripture says to prove all things (1Th 5:21).
webster_full: MISINFORMATION, n. (from 1587, OED) Incorrect or misleading information. Distinguished in modern use from disinformation, which is deliberately deceptive. From mis- + information.

Usage note: laws and policies against misinformation have in some countries been used to restrict journalistic work and limit political expression, as reported by UNESCO and other monitors (Wikipedia, “Misinformation”).
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
And they called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
corruption_summary: Misinformation was a plain word for error; it has been bent into an official label that settles a question without hearing it, and is used to silence speech rather than answer it.
corruption_paragraphs: An error is answered by evidence. A label ends the matter before the evidence is heard. When “misinformation” is pinned on a claim by the party that dislikes it, the word does the work an argument should do. Scripture names that habit: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13), and “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).

The bending is not only a matter of speech. UNESCO and other monitoring organisations report that laws and policies written against misinformation have been used in some countries to restrict journalists and limit political expression, and in some cases to imprison journalists and editors. The apostles met the same move when the council “commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus” (Act 4:18). Their answer stands: “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20). A Christian should hate falsehood, test every claim, and refuse to let the word for error become a muzzle on the truth.
roots_summary: mis- + information → misinformation (OED earliest 1587), wrong information → modern label set against disinformation → tool for restricting speech.
roots_lines: 1587: OED’s earliest evidence, a text by Abraham Fleming and others
Modern use: distinguished from disinformation by intent (Wikipedia)
January 2024: the World Economic Forum names misinformation and disinformation the most severe short-term global risks
usage: “Before you call it misinformation, show me where it is wrong.”
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. (1Th 5:21).
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. (Pro 18:13).

etymology: Formed within English from extreme and the suffix -ist, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1806, in the writing of Benjamin Moseley, physician, and lists its earliest subjects as politics and religion in the 1800s.
biblical_def: An extremist is one who holds extreme views or advocates extreme measures, especially in politics or religion. The word has always depended on a reference point: a view is extreme only measured against what the speaker, or some assumed social consensus, takes to be the mainstream. It is used descriptively by scholars and journalists, and pejoratively by opposing groups. A recent example touches Virginia directly. In 2023 an FBI Richmond Field Office assessment associated beliefs held by many Catholics with domestic extremism. A Justice Department working group later reported that FBI internal reviews concluded the product “improperly conflated religious doctrine with violent extremism.” The Christian observation: the faithful have always been called extremists by the world. Festus told Paul, “thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad,” and Paul answered, “I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness” (Act 26:24–25). Paul confessed that “after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers” (Act 24:14). And Christ warned, “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call them of his household?” (Mat 10:25).
webster_summary: One holding extreme views or advocating extreme measures, especially in politics or religion (OED earliest 1806); measured always against an assumed mainstream, and now applied to ordinary orthodox belief. “I am not mad” (Act 26:25).
webster_full: EXTREMIST, n. and adj. (from 1806, OED) One who holds extreme opinions or advocates extreme measures, especially in politics or religion. From extreme + -ist.
Usage note: the label depends on what the speaker takes to be the mainstream, and may be used pejoratively by opposing groups (Wikipedia, “Extremism”).
scriptures: And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
It is enough for the disciple that he be as his master, and the servant as his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call them of his household?
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: Extremist has no fixed measure, so whoever sets the mainstream can file ordinary orthodoxy under it; a 2023 FBI Richmond assessment associated “beliefs held by many Catholics” with domestic extremism.
corruption_paragraphs: A word that depends on a moving centre can be moved. As the public consensus drifts away from Christian morality, beliefs that every generation of the church has held are pushed, without changing, toward the edge of the map and then labelled extreme. The 2023 Richmond assessment shows how quickly the label passes from rhetoric into the files of a law-enforcement agency, and how it lumps religious doctrine together with violence.

Scripture does not let the Christian measure himself by the crowd’s centre. It warns of the opposite danger: the lukewarm church, neither cold nor hot, which Christ will spue out (Rev 3:16). The believer must reject real extremism, the hatred and violence that Scripture condemns, while refusing the label when it is pinned on truth and soberness (Act 26:25).
roots_summary: extreme + -ist → extremist (OED earliest 1806; politics and religion, 1800s) → label relative to an assumed mainstream → applied to orthodox belief (FBI Richmond, 2023).
roots_lines: 1806: OED’s earliest evidence, Benjamin Moseley; OED subjects politics and religion (1800s)
2023: FBI Richmond Field Office assessment associates beliefs held by many Catholics with domestic extremism; later removed from FBI systems (U.S. Department of Justice)
usage: “Praying outside the clinic does not make a man an extremist.”
I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness. (Act 26:25).

etymology: Formed within English from race (n.6) and the suffix -ist, perhaps modelled on a French word, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1919, in a translation by J. R. Barcos. The OED’s “perhaps” marks the French model as uncertain.
biblical_def: A racist, in the word’s established sense, is a person who holds that people of one race are inferior to another and treats them with contempt or injustice for it. The word is recent, first recorded in 1919. Scripture condemns the sin it names. God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26), and in Christ “There is neither Jew nor Greek… for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28). Partiality is sin: “if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin” (Jas 2:9), and the judge must “not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour” (Lev 19:15). The Christian observation: because the sin is real, the word matters, and so its definition matters. In his 2019 book How to Be an Antiracist, Ibram X. Kendi defined racism as any policy that creates inequitable outcomes between people of different skin colors, defined a racist as anyone who supports such policies “through their actions or inaction or expressing a racist idea,” and argued that there is no middle ground: one is either racist or antiracist.
webster_summary: One who holds another race inferior and treats its members with contempt or injustice (OED earliest 1919). Scripture condemns partiality (Jas 2:9) and teaches one blood (Act 17:26); the word has been redefined to cover unequal outcomes and mere inaction.
webster_full: RACIST, n. and adj. (from 1919, OED) One who believes that people of a particular race are inferior, and acts or speaks with contempt or partiality on that ground. From race + -ist, perhaps on a French model (OED).
Usage note: Ibram X. Kendi, How to Be an Antiracist (2019), defines racism by inequitable outcomes and a racist by support for such policies through action or inaction (Wikipedia).
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.

The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.
corruption_summary: Racist named a real sin of the heart and hand; it has been redefined to mean any support, or even inaction, toward outcomes judged unequal, so that guilt is assigned by group and by result instead of by deed.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture locates partiality in the heart and in the judgment a man makes about his neighbour (Jas 2:9; Lev 19:15). Kendi’s redefinition moves it to outcomes. Under that definition a man may be called racist without any contempt in his heart or injustice in his hand, simply for failing to support a favoured policy, and there is no neutral ground on which he can stand.

The result is a new partiality. Guilt is assigned by group membership and by statistical result, which is the very thing Ezekiel forbade: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Eze 18:20). The Christian answer is not to shrug at the sin. It is to define it as God does, to repent of it where it is truly found, and to refuse a definition that makes every man guilty by category and no man able to be forgiven.
roots_summary: race + -ist, perhaps on a French model → racist (OED earliest 1919) → contempt and partiality by race → redefined by outcomes and inaction (Kendi, 2019).
roots_lines: 1919: OED’s earliest evidence, translation by J. R. Barcos
2019: Ibram X. Kendi, How to Be an Antiracist: racism defined by inequitable outcomes; no middle ground (Wikipedia)
usage: “Contempt for a man because of his race is sin, and the church must say so.”
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin. (Jas 2:9).

etymology: Of multiple origins, partly from French progressif and partly from Latin progressivus, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence from around 1450, in Richard of Wallingford’s Exafrenon, an astronomical sense. The OED lists political and religious uses from the 1830s.
biblical_def: Progressive first meant moving forward or advancing step by step, as a heavenly body moves along its course; the OED’s earliest sense is astronomical, about 1450. It later took on senses in medicine, commerce, education and grammar, and from the 1830s in politics and religion, for those favouring change and reform. In American history the Progressive Era ran from about the 1890s to World War I or the Great Depression, and its reform movement was to a significant extent rooted in and energized by religion; the contemporary progressive movement is largely secular by comparison. The Christian observation: progress is a good word if it has a fixed destination. “The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18). But the LORD also commands, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). Paul warned of those “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2Ti 3:7).
webster_summary: Advancing step by step (OED, about 1450); in politics from the 1830s, favouring change and reform. A label that claims the future and casts opponents as backward. True progress shines more and more unto the perfect day (Pro 4:18).
webster_full: PROGRESSIVE, adj. and n. (from about 1450, OED) 1. Moving forward; advancing by stages. 2. (Politics, from the 1830s) Favouring change, reform or innovation; a person who does. From French progressif and Latin progressivus.

History note: the American Progressive Era, about the 1890s to 1917 or 1929, was to a significant extent religiously motivated; the contemporary movement is largely secular (Wikipedia, “Progressivism in the United States”).
scriptures: But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
corruption_summary: Progressive claims the future for one side: change is assumed to be advance, so the old paths are cast as backward without being shown false.
corruption_paragraphs: Progress means getting closer to a goal. A movement that names itself progressive without naming the goal has made change itself the measure, and anyone who resists the change is cast as standing in the way of the future. The word wins the argument by its grammar before a reason is given.

Scripture has a fixed destination, the perfect day of Pro 4:18, and it measures progress by nearness to it. Sometimes progress means going forward; sometimes it means turning back to the old paths that Israel refused (Jer 6:16). A people ever learning and never coming to the truth (2Ti 3:7) is not progressing at all, however fast it moves.
roots_summary: Latin progressivus / French progressif → progressive (OED about 1450, astronomy) → politics and religion (1830s) → Progressive Era (1890s–) → secular movement label.
roots_lines: About 1450: OED’s earliest evidence, Richard of Wallingford’s Exafrenon (astronomy)
1890s–1917/1929: the American Progressive Era, largely religious in motive (Wikipedia)
usage: “Calling a policy progressive does not tell you where it is going.”
Ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein. (Jer 6:16).

etymology: A compound of reproductive and health. The Oxford English Dictionary records its earliest evidence in 1893, in the London Homœopathic Hospital Reports. Reproductive itself is formed from re- and productive, with OED evidence from 1746.
biblical_def: Reproductive health in its plain sense means the health of the body’s reproductive system: fertility, pregnancy, childbirth and the conditions that affect them. It is a medical phrase more than a century old. In 1994 the United Nations International Conference on Population and Development in Cairo, attended by delegations from 179 states, placed reproductive rights at the centre of its Programme of Action. The issue of abortion was so contentious that the delegates omitted any recommendation to legalize it. Even so, during and after the conference some parties tried to read “reproductive health” as implying abortion or a right to abortion, and the European Union’s Council Presidency stated that its commitment to promoting reproductive health did not include promoting abortion. The Christian observation: the womb is the place where God forms life. “Thou hast covered me in my mother’s womb” (Psa 139:13). “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee” (Jer 1:5). “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psa 127:3).
webster_summary: The health of the reproductive system (OED earliest 1893); since the 1994 Cairo conference often used as an umbrella that some read to include abortion. The fruit of the womb is the LORD’s reward (Psa 127:3).
webster_full: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH, n. (from 1893, OED) The health of the reproductive system and its functions, including fertility, pregnancy and childbirth. Compound of reproductive + health.

Usage note: the 1994 Cairo Programme of Action made no recommendation to legalize abortion; attempts to read reproductive health as implying abortion did not reflect the conference consensus (Wikipedia, “International Conference on Population and Development”).
scriptures: For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb.
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
corruption_summary: Reproductive health is a medical phrase for the care of fertility and childbirth; it has been stretched into a euphemism that carries abortion, the ending of the very life reproduction produces, under the name of health.
corruption_paragraphs: Health is care of the body for its good. A phrase that means the health of the organs God made for bearing children has been widened to include the procedure that kills the child they bear. The euphemism works by leaving the child out of the sentence: it speaks of the mother’s system and never of the person within it.

The record of the Cairo conference itself shows the move: the delegates declined to recommend legal abortion, and yet the phrase was afterwards read as implying it. Scripture speaks plainly where the euphemism will not. The child in the womb is known and formed by God (Psa 139:13; Jer 1:5); “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13); and the church is told to deliver those drawn unto death (Pro 24:11).
roots_summary: reproductive (OED from 1746) + health → reproductive health (OED earliest 1893) → 1994 Cairo Programme of Action → contested umbrella term read to include abortion.
roots_lines: 1746: OED’s earliest evidence for reproductive, James Hervey
1994: International Conference on Population and Development, Cairo; 179 states; no recommendation to legalize abortion (Wikipedia)
usage: “Prenatal care is reproductive health; ending the pregnancy is not.”
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD. (Psa 127:3).
